value.overview: The Tufted Flycatcher is a small, active tyrant flycatcher of cool mountain forests from Mexico through Central America to northern South America. It is named for the short crest that gives its head a tufted appearance. The species often perches upright on exposed twigs, making short flights to catch insects before returning to the same perch. In Costa Rica, it is a characteristic bird of the highlands and is frequently encountered in forest edges and other partly open mountain habitats.
value.classification: The Tufted Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the large family of New World flycatchers. Its scientific name is Mitrephanes phaeocercus.
value.identification: This flycatcher is about 13 centimeters long and has a noticeable pointed crest, dark gray head and upperparts, and warm cinnamon or rufous wings and tail. The underparts are usually pale gray on the throat and breast, becoming yellowish on the belly. Its bill is broad and dark, and the overall shape is compact. In Costa Rica, its combination of a small crest, rufous wing panels, and mountain-forest habitat helps distinguish it from other small flycatchers.
value.rangeHabitat: The Tufted Flycatcher ranges from western and southern Mexico through Central America and into parts of northwestern South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in the central and southern highlands, generally from middle elevations to the upper montane zone, including areas such as the Cordillera de Tilarán, Cordillera Central, and Cordillera de Talamanca. It uses humid montane and cloud forests, woodland edges, clearings, shade-grown coffee areas, plantations, and roadsides with scattered trees, usually at roughly 900 to 3,000 meters elevation.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Tufted Flycatcher is generally a resident or local elevational migrant rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals may move upslope or downslope in response to seasonal conditions, food availability, and breeding activity. The species is present in suitable Costa Rican highland habitats throughout much of the year.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place during the rainy or early wet-season period, although timing varies across the species' broad range. The nest is typically placed in a natural cavity, an old woodpecker hole, or a similar sheltered opening, and may also be situated in a bank or other protected structure. The female lays a small clutch of pale eggs marked with darker spots. Both adults are involved in feeding the young, which are supplied mainly with captured insects.
value.dietFeeding: The Tufted Flycatcher feeds mainly on flying insects, including beetles, flies, moths, wasps, and other small arthropods. It usually hunts from a fairly exposed perch, making quick sallies into the air to seize prey and then returning to the same or a nearby perch. It also takes insects from vegetation and may occasionally eat small fruits or other plant material, especially when insect prey is less available.
value.behavior: This species is alert and energetic, commonly sitting upright on exposed branches while flicking its wings or tail. It defends feeding and breeding territories with calls and short aerial pursuits. The Tufted Flycatcher often forages alone or in pairs but may join mixed-species feeding flocks in mountain forests. Its call is a sharp, high-pitched note, and its short, repeated flights from a regular perch make it relatively conspicuous in suitable habitat.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains common or fairly common in many appropriate highland areas, including parts of Costa Rica.
